epithet: The slanderer, and what his wealth will buy him
lede: A portrait in three strokes: he mocks people to their faces, cuts at them behind their backs, and counts his money as though it could keep him alive. Then the door closes on him — literally.

names.name: al-Humazah
names.note: After the first of the two words it opens with. Humazah and lumazah are both intensive forms: one who makes a habit of wounding people — by word or by gesture, in their presence or their absence. The commentators give several ways of telling the two apart, and all of them are true of the same man.

revelation.detail: Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī both record agreement that it is Makkan; Ibn al-Jawzī notes one isolated saying that it is Madinan. The commentators differ only over whether it came down about one man or about a type.
revelation.when: The early years in Makkah, when the believers were mocked in the streets by the men of standing

evidence.quote: وَهِيَ مَكِّيَّةٌ بِإجْماعِهِمْ قالَ هِبَةُ اللَّهِ المُفَسِّرُ: وقَدْ قِيلَ: إنَّها مَدَنِيَّةٌ
تَفْسِيرُ سُورَةِ "الْهُمَزَةِ" مَكِّيَّةٌ بِإِجْمَاعٍ. وَهِيَ تِسْعُ آيات

setting: The first Muslims in Makkah were, many of them, poor, young, enslaved or without a clan to protect them. The men who opposed the Prophet ﷺ were the opposite of all that, and one of their weapons cost them nothing: ridicule. A wink as a believer walked past; a remark for the others to laugh at; a story told once he had gone.

The commentators name the men it was said to be about, and the list is itself a picture of the opposition: al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq, in the report from Ibn ʿAbbās; al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil; al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah; Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who tortured Bilāl. Others, Mujāhid among them, said it was not sent down about anyone in particular but about everyone of this description — and the wording supports them: “every” slanderer.

What ties the two halves of his character together is the fourth ayah’s diagnosis. He gathers wealth and counts it over because he thinks it will make him permanent. A man who believes that has nothing to fear from anyone, and so he says what he likes about them.

occasions.title: One man, or every such man
occasions.text: Ibn al-Jawzī sets out the difference. Those who say it came down about a particular person name, among others, al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq — the report of Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās — and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil. Those who say it is general take it as it reads.
occasions.source: Ibn al-Jawzī, Zād al-Masīr, at the head of the surah.

evidence.quote: واخْتَلَفَ المُفَسِّرُونَ هَلْ نَزَلَتْ في حَقِّ شَخْصٍ بِعَيْنِهِ، أمْ نَزَلَتْ عامَّةً؟ عَلى قَوْلَيْنِ. أحَدُهُما: نَزَلَتْ في حَقِّ شَخْصٍ بِعَيْنِهِ. ثُمَّ فِيهِ سِتَّةُ أقْوالٍ. أحَدُها: الأخْنَسُ بْنُ شَرِيقٍ، رَواهُ أبُو صالِحٍ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ

aim: A threat to those who look down on the religion and its people, and mock them.

outline.title: The man
outline.summary: Woe to every slanderer and backbiter, who has gathered wealth and counted it, thinking that his wealth will make him live for ever.

outline.title: His end
outline.summary: No — he will be flung into the Crusher. And what will make you know what the Crusher is? The fire of Allah, kindled, which rises over the hearts — the place where the contempt began. It is closed in upon them, in columns stretched out.

keyAyah.why: The surah’s charge, in its first breath. Only two surahs open with “woe”; the other is al-Muṭaffifīn.

before: Al-ʿAṣr said that all people are at a loss but a few. Al-Humazah is a close study of one who is.
after: This man thought his wealth would preserve him. Al-Fīl is the story of an army that thought its strength would — and of what became of it within sight of Makkah.
